---
title: "The layout"
subtitle: "What's in each folder of a real game, and why it's split that way."
---

Open `field-guide/minus80/snail-assassin/` in your editor. At the top level:

```
snail-assassin/
├── index.html         the page (with a rotate hint and a screen-reader region)
├── package.json       scripts: dev, build, test, lint, format, check
├── vite.config.ts     a fixed port per game, relative paths, test settings
├── tsconfig.json      TypeScript settings
├── eslint.config.js   lint rules
├── .node-version      26
├── CHANGELOG.md       what changed in each version
├── docs/              design, science, accessibility, playtesting, art, roadmap
├── public/            files served as-is (icon, web app manifest)
├── src/               the game
└── tests/             unit tests
```

Compare *Cold Chain*'s folder: `index.html`, `package.json`, `vite.config.js`, `public/`, `src/`. Everything else here is there because more than one person works on the game, over months, and it has to keep working.

## Inside `src/`

```
src/
├── main.ts          builds the game from the list of scenes
├── config/          gameConfig.ts (size, palette), tuning.ts (gameplay numbers), settings.ts (saved options)
├── scenes/          nine scenes: Boot, Splash, Title, Settings, Select, Hunt, Pause, Results, Discovery
├── systems/         the rules: hunt, fish, predator, venom, movement... pure TypeScript, no Phaser
├── characters/      the three playable snails, as data
├── entities/        Reef: the drawn background
├── input/           keyboard and touch → the same "input" object
├── ui/              buttons, the HUD, text styles, screen-reader announcements
├── audio/           a sound engine that synthesises every effect
├── content/         the player-facing science text
├── debug/           a balancing panel, only in development
└── utils/           small helpers: vector maths, random numbers
```

## Three layers

The folders fall into three layers, and the arrows only point one way:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 9
flowchart LR
  I["input/<br/>keys, touch"] --> S["scenes/<br/>Phaser: draw, play sounds, switch screens"]
  S --> R["systems/<br/>the rules, as plain data and functions"]
  C["config/, characters/<br/>numbers and data"] --> R
```

- **Systems** decide *what happens*: where the fish swim, when the octopus notices you, how much venom is left. They know nothing about Phaser, screens or keyboards.
- **Scenes** decide *how it looks and sounds*: they ask the systems what happened and draw it.
- **Input** turns devices into one plain object (`HuntInput`), so the rules never care whether you used a key or a finger.

*Cold Chain* has the same three ideas, mixed together in `Play.js`: the thaw rules sit right next to the camera shake. At 300 lines that's fine. At 4,500 it isn't, and [the hunt](04-hunt.qmd) shows what the separation buys.

## The entry point

{{< snippet repo="minus80" file="snail-assassin/src/main.ts" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The same shape as *Cold Chain*'s `main.js` ([lesson 7](../lessons/07-scenes.qmd#the-five-scenes)): import the scenes, list them, make the game. Two extras: the game config is built by a function in `config/gameConfig.ts`, and the canvas gets accessibility attributes so a screen reader can describe it.
:::
